Hon. Warren Allmand (Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine
East): Mr. Speaker, as you know, we are presently debating four amendments which would strike out four clauses of Bill C-130, the Bill to implement the Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement. Those clauses that we wish to delete from the legislation are clauses dealing with the dispute settlement mechanism. The reason we want to delete those clauses from the Bill is because they are totally inadequate. They fall far short of what was pursued by the Government when it started its negotiations with the United States.
As a matter of fact, not only are they inadequate, but in some respects they give Canada less than we had under the GATT arrangements. Under the GATT arrangements in certain instances we were able to challenge the fairness of U.S. trade laws such as certain types of anti-dumping and countervailing laws. We were able to challenge the very fairness of those laws.
However, under this agreement and this dispute settlement mechanism we cannot challenge the fairness of those American trade laws. We can only challenge whether or not those laws are being administered fairly, whether the administration has been done correctly and whether the correct procedures have been followed. The laws themselves cannot be challenged.
When the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry (Mr. Axworthy) was discussing this, he provoked a response from the Parliamentary Secretary who attempted to contradict him and said that we were not prevented from using GATT remedies under the agreement and under the legislation. That is not so.
Article 1801.2 of Chapter 18 states:
Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement
Disputes arising under both this Agreement and the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade, and agreements negotiated thereunder, may be settled in either forum, according to the rules of that forum-
Article 1801.1 states:
Except for the matters covered in Chapter Seventeen (Financial Services) and Chapter Nineteen (Binational Dispute Settlement in Antidumping and Countervailing Duty Cases), the provisions of this Part shall apply-
This part should only apply to those matters which do not fall under Chapter Seventeen and Chapter Nineteen. Chapter Nineteen deals with countervail and anti-dumping.
If we look at Chapter Nineteen we see that it states:
Each Party reserves the right to apply its antidumping law and countervailing duty law to goods imported from the territory of the other Party.
It then goes on to state that the review of final anti-dumping and countervailing duty determination shall be determined by the process as set out in Chapter Nineteen.
With respect to countervail and anti-dumping, we cannot use the dispute settlement mechanism under GATT. That is exempted by Article 1 of 1801. The Parliamentary Secretary should pay close attention to that.
In addition, and more important, there was a GATT decision in 1949 which stated: "The determination of rights and obligations between Governments arising under a bilateral agreement is not a matter within the competence of the contracting parties", meaning under GATT. During the intervening 39 years since that decision, a dispute arising from a bilateral agreement has not been heard.
By adopting these dispute settlement procedures we lose our right to question countervailing laws and anti-dumping laws under the GATT. With respect to the fairness of those laws under GATT, we are restricted to the dispute settlement mechanism in this legislation. The dispute settlement mechanism under this legislation only deals with how the laws are administered, not with the fairness of the laws themselves.

Those are the barriers to the United States which have really been troubling Canadian business.
All Canadians are familiar with the softwood lumber case, the shakes and shingles case, the East Coast fish case, the potash case and the steel case. All those were cases of countervail and anti-dumping. They were not cases of tariff duties.
Since 1979 until the beginning of this year there have been 300 countervail cases in the United States directed at Canadian business. In 70 per cent of those cases the American tribunals found injury against Canadian businesses. This means that a countervail duty was added in 70 per cent of those 300 cases.
That is the principal problem with trade between Canada and the United States. It is a non-tariff barrier. It has not been dealt with in this agreement. These dispute settlement mechanisms do not provide the sort of relief from those laws that we would like and that the Canadian people would like. As a matter of fact, that is what the Prime Minister wanted when he started the whole business.
I was amused when the Hon. Member from Edmonton- and I forget what part of Edmonton he is from-spoke just a few moments ago. As a matter of fact, at this very moment 80 per cent of all trade in goods and services in Canada and the United States are without tariff. That is brought down from a point after the Second World War when a high percentage of the goods and services exchanged between Canada and the United States were subject to tariff. Not only have we eliminated tariffs on 80 per cent of all goods and services, but the average rate of tariff has come down from about 30 per cent to about 5 per cent on that remaining 20 per cent.
Because we are opposing this agreement, and because we are opposing this dispute settlement mechanism, it does not mean that we are opposed to freer trade. We are saying that the system that was in place before this agreement was a better system, and we did not give up our independence, our identity, and our sovereignty to get a few trifles thrown at us by the United States Government.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if we consider all the attacks on the free trade agreement, it is clear that ignorance, not understanding, is gaining ground, and that is why we have to get involved in this debate because of the way the facts are being misrepresented.
Basically, the FTA is a deal. A deal is an agreement signed by two consenting parties, and it is often a comprehensive whole. The various components, what we call the package, are all part of the deal or agreement. It's like going to a store, Mr. Speaker, and buying a dozen eggs. We don't buy a dozen yolks one day, a dozen whites the next and the shells the day after. They are all part of the same package!
A deal is exactly the same, but let me explain. As a Government, we have every right to stop letting our neighbours push us around and to establish-because basically, the FTA is mainly that-a tribunal to arbitrate any trade disputes that may exist between our two countries, because already 85 per cent of our goods cross our borders unrestricted. There is thus the remaining 15 per cent. What we are doing, Mr. Speaker, is establish an impartial tribunal.
What was the situation like before? We had our problems with cedar shakes, softwood lumber, pork, mustard seed and lobster, all goods that were protected by our neighbours to the south. When we went before the courts, we sent a battery of lawyers to Washington to defend our interests before U.S. tribunals under U.S. law. Mr. Speaker, we will have an impartial tribunal that will hand down decisions, that will have its own rules and conduct its own investigations, and that is what sovereignty and autonomy are all about.
I was talking to one of my colleagues on the weekend about acid rain, and this person said: Sure, but we can force the Americans to do something about acid rain. So I said: Aren't you satisfied with what the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) told the U.S. Congress? He was the first Prime Minister to do that. He said: Sure, but that doesn't help! So I said: It will help eventually, and what are we supposed to do when our neighbours to the south who are individualists and have their own parliamentary system and their own political and intellectual way of doing things, what do we do if they won't budge? Do we shoot down one of their planes? Do we shoot down the first plane that crosses the border? No. This is a democratic country, and so we pass legislation that will enable both countries to reach an agreement.
I repeat, 85 per cent of our goods cross the border without any customs interference because . . . Now look at the free trade agreement. I explained about the tribunal. The agreement is concerned with four specific points in particular. It concerns tariffs on about 15 per cent of the goods that now

August 22, 1988
Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement
cross our borders; it concerns export and import quotas; it concerns laws, so-called malicious laws that while ostensibly protecting one product, prevent others from entering the country; and it concerns incentives. But basically, how much trade is there between Canada and the United States? Our trade is worth $169 billion annually, and 80 to 85 per cent is with our neighbours to the south.
So we set up a free trade agreement, and all of a sudden some people get terribly upset. That's it, we will have to start exporting. Not any more than we used to. We are an exporting country. We were before the free trade agreement. Mr. Speaker, we export 33 to 34 per cent of our Gross National Product. For instance, the Japanese export about 10 per cent of their GNP. We have to export because we have a small population, 25, 26 or 27 million. But we always had a problem because our markets were not stable.
Remember in 1984 or early 1985, when hog producers in the riding of Beauharnois-Salaberry came to my office because the United States had levied a tariff on pork carcases which were exported by the pound, 5 cents a pound, I think it was $1 per head? So what was the result? It meant that hog producers were stuck with their pigs, and they couldn't sell them anymore. Why? For the simple reason that producers in the U.S. went to see their lobbyists, their politicians and they said: Listen, Canadian pork producers with their Canadian laws and their provincial legislation can produce more cheaply. So you have to stop this, it doesn't make sense. So we had another outburst! There was a problem with lobster and with softwood lumber. It took so long with the softwood lumber dispute, Mr. Speaker-every time we had to go to the United States and defend our case before the U. S. courts. The free trade agreement will establish an international court, and we have every right to do that.
Earlier, some people said we were "shafted" by U.S. protectionist legislation. Certainly not! That particular legislation does not abolish the tribunal set up under the FTA. We are talking about leadership, Mr. Speaker. Just now they were saying, "Call an election and you will see. Campaign on it!" Talk about leadership. We will talk about leadership right now with the NDP.
Mr. Speaker, a by-election was held about a month ago in Lac-Saint-Jean. The NDP had great figures-they are perfect, so perfect they are almost unassailable-but they did not even get 9 per cent of the vote in a riding where normally they should have had more, according to the opinion polls. So let's have an election! The president of the Quebec wing of the NDP did not even get 2 per cent of the vote in the riding of Johnson. They were not even able to put up with Toupin besides, and now they want to go to the people, Mr. Speaker! Let us have an election. We will call an election on that, because the Prime Minister of Canada, Mr. Speaker, has shown leadership with the Free Trade Agreement, the Meech Lake Agreement and the various tough issues he has had to negotiate! And that is what people will have to judge, leadership and nothing else!
I remember the day after . . . Where does the Free Trade Agreement come from? You remember that the Liberal Party set up a Royal Commission chaired by Mr. Macdonald; the President of the Liberal Party of Canada, lawyer Michel Robert, was on it. They presented a report. I remember the journalists' reaction when this report was tabled in the House. Do you know what they said? They said that Mr. Mulroney would have to stop eating Big Macs and have a real meal. My God, here is a Government that has had a real meal. . . For once a Royal Commission report was not shelved, $20 million was not spent for nothing . .. ! The Prime Minister digested it and moved the negotiations forward, because he asserted the leadership he should as Prime Minister of Canada.
Mr. Speaker, in the next election campaign, despite all the trickery, half-truths and ignorance which are having an impact, as I said at the beginning, Canadians will still believe that Canada was built on trade, because we already export 32 or 33 per cent of our gross national product. That is important! We built on that and now we will have an agreement to stabilize it. People who want to attack free trade wrap themselves in the flag and masquerade as true nationalists. Mr. Speaker, they say our culture is at risk. Our culture is not at risk because of free trade. Our culture is at risk because of what we see on television every day. Every day we see American culture, and that is much worse than the free trade agreement. We don't care about that. Of course I don't want to stop magazines and journals at the border. But those are the vehicles of cultural change, not the changes in our trade rules. Certainly not! In fact, those rules may enhance our culture because we are going to be able to defend ourselves under Canadian law before a tribunal that will be recognized by both countries. That may do a lot more to enhance our Canadian identity, our Canadian culture and our Canadian heritage.
Mr. Speaker, the short tempers of our friends opposite have often led to stormy debates here in the House. I will always remember when we had the softwood lumber affair and the pork exports. So what did the Government do? Instead of taking to our guns and settling accounts with our neighbours, we introduced legislation that would provide for economic and trade stability. Mr. Speaker, that is FTA. It is no more than that because when it comes down to it, 85 per cent of our goods already cross the border free of customs duty.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to rise again in my place to debate the amendments in group nine put forward by our trade critic, the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry (Mr. Axworthy). In this group of amendments we are addressing the question of the settlement dispute mechanism.
In 1983, when the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) ran for the Tory leadership, he put aside any fears that a party led by him would enter free trade negotiations with the U.S. That was very clear and categorical. In 1984, during the last federal
August 22, 1988

election, there was no national debate on a bilateral trade agreement with the U.S. Notwithstanding those facts, the Prime Minister's most compelling reason for entering into these negotiations with the U.S. was the need to obtain secure access to the American market for Canadian goods.
Then it was the Prime Minister who suggested that an agreement that would not have a binding dispute settlement mechanism, one which would exempt Canada from harassment by American trade remedy laws, would not be worth the paper it was written on. Those are the Prime Minister's words. That is not something the Opposition is saying. It was an undertaking to this country by the Prime Minister of Canada. In fact, on March 16, 1987, the Prime Minister said in this House, and I quote:
Our highest priority is to have an agreement that ends the threat to Canadian industry from U.S. protectionists who harass and restrict our exports through the misuse of trade remedy laws. Let me leave no doubt that first, a new regime on trade remedy laws must be part of the agreement.
Later, in an interview with The Wall Street Journal on April 2, he said:
The U.S. trade remedy laws cannot apply to Canada.
What have we got now? It seems very clear to one and all that after months and months of discussions the Canadian negotiators were not able to secure access to American markets for Canadian goods. Second, Canada did not obtain an exemption from U.S. trade remedy laws. If one needs to have that point made clearly, one does not have to go beyond the words of the U.S. trade representative, Clayton Yeutter, who, in reviewing the so-called free trade agreement, had this to say:
The United States countervailing duty and anti-dumping laws, defined as U.S. statutes, legislative history, regulation, administrative practice and court decisions, will remain intact and unchanged. Hence, U.S. petitioners will retain all their rights under existing U.S. laws as Canadian industries will keep their rights under Canadian law.
What did Canada obtain after months of negotiations and jetting back and forth between the two capitals? The Government said the priority was a binding dispute settlement mechanism. Yet what we have come up with is a mechanism void of any real protection for Canadian interests. First, we have a panel that can arbitrate and simply determine whether the process was followed, without looking at the fact that the process is very seriously and rigidly flawed. The panels will not be insulated from political pressure. There will be two representatives from both the U.S. and Canada and a fifth member chosen by some unknown procedure. That will not produce an objective result such as we see in GATT where most if not all of the members on the various panels who have to render dispute decisions are taken from countries not involved in the dispute.
Second, the national panels involved in anti-dumping and countervailing duty cases will have only judicial review power. They will have to look at whether the process was followed as opposed to looking at the facts underlying the dispute in the first place.
Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement
Third, anti-dumping and countervailing duty decisions by national panels will be based only on domestic law. That again leaves Canada open to future protectionist sentiments in the U.S.
Fourth, the panel procedures will be long and costly.
Fifth, panel decisions will not be binding and therefore, with the exception of safeguards, decisions will not be binding unless both parties agree beforehand to comply with the decision.
Canada's retaliatory capacity against the U.S. is weakened in the face of overwhelming harassment from a country that is much larger than ours, much more powerful economically. Who would win that war is quite obvious from the outset.
Perhaps the most important point is that our ability to dispute arrangements in trade with the Americans vis-a-vis GATT will in effect be closed off because GATT will not get into a position of rendering a decision taken between countries in a bilateral agreement. A number of government Members suggested that we are still living under GATT rules and we will be able to access GATT with respect to any harassment by the U.S. Yet a 1949 GATT decision held that the determination of rights and obligations between Governments arising under a bilateral agreement, such as the one we have now, is a matter within the competence of the contracting parties.
Therefore, we have the various components of the Canadian economy added to the cultural and communications industries which are under pressure in this agreement on the one hand.
On the other hand, we do not have a dispute settlement mechanism which can enforce and defend our own interests. Canadians are obviously worried about entering into an arrangement which seems to be lopsided, one way, and doomed in terms of advancing and enhancing our trade numbers vis-avis the Americans.
We have moved these two amendments in order to draw the attention of Canadians to the ills of this dispute settling system which has been put in place by the negotiators of the Canadian Government. They have not realized the first objective of the Prime Minister and are trying to cover that up with various other aspects and colourful language. However, when you remove the rhetoric, you are left with a fragile agreement and a dispute settlement mechanism which certainly does not build the confidence which our industries and our country and its people require and deserve.
It is with that interest in mind that we are trying to get the Government to focus honestly and competently on trying to provide a dispute settlement mechanism which will not only talk about equity and defence but will deliver on both those fronts.

The fact is, Mr. Speaker, the amendment we are bringing forward is an important corollary to those amendments we have just debated. It is a very important amendment because it establishes a very distinct difference in the way in which we view trade policy in this country. It is very simple. The Conservative Party of Canada, the Republican Party of the north, the Party that believes in all those great fond dreams of Ronald Reagan, has a very simple principle. It is going to abandon the time tested and effective procedures we used in the past to protect Canadian trading interests both in negotiating with the GATT and at the same time using the dispute settlement mechanism. We, on the other hand, believe that Canada has prospered, our trade has expanded, and our opportunities abroad have been developed by relying upon the international trading system. It is a very clear difference between the two. It is not a matter of who is for or against more trade. It is a question of how do we do it.
How do we ensure security of access? How do we open access up? How do we diversify trade? The Conservative Party, the Republican Party of the north, has clearly adopted the position that they are going to plight their troth and sign the marriage certificate with the United States. We have heard them talk about it: we have to join a market of 100 million people, we have to get behind these walls because those Europeans are after us and the Japanese are after us, and we have to sort of sign up with Uncle Sam. That was the position taken by the Minister for International Trade (Mr. Crosbie) and his family 30 years ago. I suppose if consistency is a virtue, he has one virtue at least. He has been consistent on that. Unfortunately, it is now an argument that has been adopted by the Conservative Party of Canada.
We are saying that our position is very different. We want to establish a trading vision that has a much broader base than that, one that looks at it on a global basis and recognizes that in negotiating an agreement one never gets oneself in a position as Mr. Reisman, who was the chief negotiator said, where one has to put on the table far more benefits than the other side is prepared to offer because they have a larger market. Mr. Reisman said that. He said that was the reason we had to put water on the table. He said in his famous speech in front of the Ontario Economic Council: "When you are asking for a change and you are negotiating with a power that is 10 times your size and you are trying to get some similarity in trade benefits, you have to put chips on the table that are non-trade chips". So we put on investment, we put on energy, we put on resources, and we put on water, in order to get some changes in the trade area.

Mr. Speaker, I get a very big kick out of listening to the Hon. Member who puts his own interpretation on the agreement that we have signed.
In the overview of the agreement it is laid out very well. It states that the agreement sets a new standard for trade agreements concluded under the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade. If we were dismissing the GATT would we conclude this agreement under the GATT? Of course we would not. What this agreement does, and it says here, is that
Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement
it takes various GATT commitments, bilateral arrangements, and ad hoc understandings and transforms them into a treaty based relationship between Canada and the United States which should govern the trade and economic relationship for the foreseeable future. The agreement meets the test of fairness and of mutual advantage.
It also states that this accord sends a powerful signal against protectionism and trade liberalization. It reflects the commitment of both Governments to liberalize trade on a global basis through multilateral trade negotiations under the GATT. All the way through this agreement the GATT rules are mentioned in chapter after chapter.
Let us talk about Article 1902 in the agreement which considers anti-dumping and countervail duty law. It considers the right of either party to amend its anti-dumping or countervail law and to bring in amendments to its anti-dumping or countervail duty law provided that in the case of amendment to a party's anti-dumping or countervailing duty statute-and it goes through a list of requirements, one being such amendments shall apply to goods from the other party only if such application is specified in the amending statute. It goes on and on. Under Section 2(d) of Article 1902 it is stated:
d) such amendment, as applicable to the other Party, is not inconsistent with i) the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade-
For the Hon. Member to stand up here to say that this Government has dismissed the GATT, that we have ignored the GATT, that we are not paying any attention to it, is totally wrong. The Hon. Member knows that full well. He knows that the Government has been on a two-track process on trade, both on a bilateral basis with our largest trading partner and on a multilateral basis with the GATT. As a matter of fact, we Canadians can be very proud in the leading role that we have been taking in the negotiations, the Uruguay Round of the GATT negotiations which are ongoing at the present time and which are almost at the half-way point. However, as we know, these negotiations can go on for a number of years. It is interesting to listen to the Hon. Member talk about us not being committed to GATT. Of course we are committed to GATT.
I listened to him say that Manitoba is in such financial bad shape that it will never recover. Manitoba has the second lowest unemployment rate in Canada. The Hon. Member should be proud of that. With this free trade agreement it will accomplish a lot more. There is no question about it. Let me read for the record an editorial from The Financial Post entitled "Hardly a sell-out". It reads:
As Trade Minister John Crosbie noted in the House the other day, it's curious that the Opposition wants to move about 100 amendments to a trade bill they say they will tear up if elected.

Meanwhile, the general criticism of the Free Trade Agreement continues. The Government "doesn't have a mandate to take this country into the U.S.," the NDP's Steven Langdon says. Liberal Leader John Turner still uses that wonderfully original line about making Canada "the 51st state." (As we have said before, we wish he could accord the whole of Canada more equivalency than Rhode Island, but he's stuck on 51.)
As trade lawyer Christopher Thomas notes on the page opposite, Turner also characterizes the FTA as the "Sale of Canada Act." The problem is, as Thomas says, the agreement offers no evidence of a sellout. The critics give the impression that Canada simply signed away the store, and the Americans committed to nothing. But, as Thomas says, "the vast majority of the agreement's terms are mutually binding."
For the most part, exceptions to the mutually binding terms arise from terms of the General Agreement on Tariffs & Trade, to which both Canada and the U.S. are parties, or from particular legislative or regulatory provisions in each country. For example, under the FTA, obligations affecting wine and spirits apply mainly to Canada.
That's because, of the two parties, only Canada is breaching its GATT obligations by discriminating against foreign alcoholic beverages.
That refers to the discriminatory pricing of the provinces. It continues:
In the area of financial services, different obligations are imposed on the two countries because of the different regulatory regimes and the different paces of deregulation.
If the free trade critics would view the agreement in the light of our GATT obligations and the legislative and regulatory provisions in each country, it becomes a less ominous piece of work. Hardly, in other words, the "bill of sale" Turner thinks it is.
That was an editorial in The Financial Post on August 22, 1988. It points out very well that this agreement is GATT consistent, that it was negotiated under the GATT rules, that this Government fully supports GATT, works with it, and as a matter of fact is playing a very leading role in the GATT negotiations that are going on now. This country can be extremely proud of the leadership role that it has taken in the agricultural end of things where there are major problems throughout the world.
It is evident to anyone who understands and who has read the free trade agreement, and it is understood that it is consistent under the GATT regulations. Under that section we can challenge a decision of the United States that it made pursuant to such anti-dumping or countervailing duty law before the binational dispute panel.

It has not been tariffs for several years now. The most serious and harassing trade barriers have been countervail and anti-dumping. As a matter of fact, I will put the following figures on the record. Since 1979 the Americans have launched 300 countervail cases against Canadians doing business in the United States. In 70 per cent of those 300 cases they found injury against these Canadian business. That means that American tribunals found that the Canadian products being sold in the United States were in some way or another subsidized, according to their laws, and therefore they added a countervail duty on to the price of the Canadian product and set up that type of barrier. The Americans awarded a countervail duty against those Canadian products in 70 per cent of 300 cases.
I also pointed out that when the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) started the free trade negotiations with the United States he stated that his highest priority was to get rid of American trade laws, such as countervail and anti-dumping. That was his highest priority on March 6, 1987. He did not accomplish that because after the negotiations were finished and the agreement was signed, Clayton Yeutter, the President's trade representative in the negotiations stated: "The U.S. countervailing duty and anti-dumping laws, defined as U.S. statutes, legislative history, regulations, administrative
August 22, 1988

practice, and court decisions-will remain intact and unchanged. Hence U.S. petitioners will retain all their rights under existing U.S. laws as Canadian industries will keep their rights under Canadian law".
The United States laws on countervail and anti-dumping remain, despite the wish of the Prime Minister that this should be done away with in the negotiations.
With respect to the dispute settlement mechanism that was set up to deal with these things, P. W. Slayton, a trade lawyer with the Toronto law firm of Blake, Cassels and Graydon stated: "Anti-dumping and countervailing duty laws remain the same in both countries. This is disappointing. Relief from United States application of its anti-dumping and countervailing duty laws was thought to be one of Canada's objectives".
That did not take place. We have moved that the dispute settlement mechanism set up in the legislation be disposed of, taken out of the legislation, and replaced with the GATT procedures.
Under GATT procedures one is allowed to question the fairness of the laws themselves, whereas under the dispute settlement mechanism that is provided for in the agreement and in the legislation, one can only question the fairness of the application of the law, and whether American law is applied fairly in accordance with its own procedures. One cannot question whether or not the law itself is fair. When I attempted to point out to government Members that this was provided for in the agreement, they attempted to rebut what I said by pointing out that each country is allowed to amend its countervail laws, but any amendment to countervail laws must be consistent with the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade.
They referred to Article 1902 of the agreement. Well, to establish that you will have a separate dispute settlement mechanism is not inconsistent with the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade. They tried to imply that it would be inconsistent. Well, it is not inconsistent. As a matter of fact, my hon. colleague and I have both referred to a decision of GATT in 1949. The 1949 GATT decision read: "The determination of rights and obligations between Governments arising under a bilateral agreement is not a matter within the competence of the contracting parties; i.e. to GATT". Since 1949, GATT has not established one panel to examine a dispute arising from a bilateral agreement. Where countries have got together and had a bilateral agreement to deal with disputes between them, GATT says: "From that point on, we do not deal with it".
What is wrong with this agreement is that the dispute settlement mechanism under the bilateral agreement says that you cannot question the fairness of the countervail and antidumping law. You can only question the fairness of its application.
Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement
It is interesting to note that the Parliamentary Secretary did not answer me nor did he answer the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry (Mr. Axworthy) with respect to that GATT decision in 1949. We asked him to explain his position with respect to that GATT decision in 1949, but he never mentioned one word with respect to it, and he cannot. There has not been one panel under GATT to deal with countries that have a bilateral dispute mechanism between them since 1949, and that is 39 years now.
Maybe the Parliamentary Secretary is listening to this somewhere else. How is it that in the softwood lumber case, when we had the problem with the United States, they did not refer it to the GATT tribunal for a resolution? They ignored the procedures under GATT. It is possible, if they had gone to GATT, they would have got a much better decision in favour of Canada than they finally worked out with the United States in the agreement they signed with them. They might have been able to get a ruling through GATT which declared the American countervail duty against our softwood lumber to be an unfair ruling. They did not go that way. We just had the Parliamentary Secretary say a few minutes ago that the Conservative Government believes very strongly in GATT. They support GATT all along the line. Well, their actions speak louder than words. When it came time to go to GATT on the softwood lumber case, they did not go to GATT.
I repeat, the dispute settlement mechanism in this agreement is not acceptable. It is not acceptable because it does not allow us to question unfair American laws relating to countervail and anti-dumping. That is why we want the dispute settlement mechanism in this agreement replaced by the GATT procedures which allow us to question not only the application of the unfair laws but the unfair laws themselves.
As my hon. colleague from Winnipeg-Fort Garry said, if the Conservative Government really believes in the provisions of GATT, really believes that we should be able to question the fairness of anti-dumping laws and countervail laws, then let it vote for this amendment tomorrow when the votes take place.

What we have said is that it is the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) of this country who started on the quest for the great trade agreement which was to emerge. various vegetable products. That has been what we have been attacking, because the Government said that it would achieve this goal, and it failed to achieve the goal. It is that failure of the Government which is at the heart of the judgment that we have to make about this deal.
I think that the crucial issues with respect to this debate are not in fact being talked about. Though we support this amendment, I think the present GATT framework of dispute settlement is not really very satisfactory. It takes a great deal of time and it is something which we as a country, for instance, could actually win in a dispute but cannot be certain that the other country will be bound by the decision which is made. There are problems with the GATT dispute system.
The point about GATT is that GATT is and was the superior form in which to try to deal with our problems with the United States. GATT gave us the possibility of being able, through negotiation in the present round in which all the GATT countries are taking part, to have the chance to put in some disciplines on the way that the United States is using its countervail system against smaller countries like Canada to block out the products from this country when they become too competitive, too readily able to out-compete the United States products against which they are being sold.
At the present stage, the Americans have a system of countervail which is totally laughable when one thinks about it. They say that if Canada is guilty of putting a subsidy on a factory when it is established, like the Michelin Tire factory in Nova Scotia, it is possible for the United States to put a countervailing duty against tires coming into the United States. It is possible for the Americans to do so because we have put a subsidy into the building of the factory. They do not look at the question of whether they subsidize their tire factories. They do not look at the question of whether fishermen in the United States are subsidized when there are subsidy and countervail actions taken against our fishermen. Those questions are not looked at because American law says that it does not have to look at those questions.
All the U.S. has to look at is whether there are subsidies used in Canada, in Germany, or in Japan. If that is the case, then the United States using its countervail system can put up a special barrier to block profits from countries being able to get access easily into the United States for their products. That is what has to change, Mr. Speaker.

On the one hand the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) went to New York in April of last year and, in an interview with The Wall Street Journal, said that U.S. trade remedy laws cannot apply to Canada. On the other hand Clayton Yeutter, the chief U.S. trade representative, when he revised the summary of the agreement which we are debating here tonight, said that U.S. countervailing duty and anti-dumping law will remain intact and unchanged. This is a complete contradiction of what our Prime Minister said 18 months earlier in New York when interviewed by The Wall Street Journal.
Under the proposed Bill we will no longer be able to dispute the fairness of the law, we will only be able to dispute the application of the law. I submit that that is a very serious departure and that it can be very dangerous for future Canadian interest in the legislation.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in examining the very complex and sometimes very technical issues surrounding the trade debate, it is important that at times we bring it back to the basics of people's livelihoods, their jobs, their income, their industry and their commitment across the country. The amendments we have presented focus very clearly on a matter of concern to people in the agricultural community.
If I might, I will quote a statement which appeared in the Portage paper in the riding held by the Minister of State for Grains and Oilseeds (Mr. Mayer). The article reports a statement made by Mr. Archie McLean, Vice-President of McCain Food, the largest Canadian-owned food processing industry. The article reads:
Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement
McLean said the agreement, which would eliminate most trade barriers between the two countries over 10 years, is a disaster for Canadian farmers and for workers in factories that process farm produce.
"We're going to survive and thrive as a corporation," he said. "We can pick up our factories and go south, but our farmers cannot do that and our factory workers cannot do that."
Under free trade, processing companies will want to buy cheaper U.S. potatoes, McLean said. And they won't want to pay the shipping costs to move them from American farms to plants in Canada, he added.
"If you look around the world, you will find most french fry factories are near growers."
McLean said about 720,000 Canadians work on farms and in food processing and one-quarter of those jobs could disappear as a result of the trade deal.
He said Canada's geography and climate make it impossible for it to compete with the United States in the food industry and he suggested agriculture be exempt from the agreement.
The article continues with further statements by Mr. McLean. Mr. McLean was a member of the advisory group which we were told was closely consulted. I have in my possession a letter which he wrote to the former Minister for International Trade, the Member for Vancouver Centre (Miss Carney), in which he declared that he was a hard-core Tory. He did not say he was a New Democrat, a Socialist, a Liberal, or a Grit. He was a Tory. He said that as a Tory he could say that the trade deal is a disaster. One must assume that he is not speaking from a partisan point of view but from a concern about his industry.
The town of Portage la Prairie, a nice community in the central part of Manitoba, is going to lose its largest industry, and not because Canadians cannot compete, are not entrepreneurs, or are not adventuresome, but because of a thing called climate. Portage la Prairie has temperatures of 20 and 30 degrees below in the winter. We have to put big bins up and pump heat into them in order to keep things warm. Due to our geography we do not grow a couple of crops a year. We have transportation costs.
As a result, if you buy your potatoes further south you can get them for about $90 a tonne. In Portage la Prairie they cost $120 a tonne and in New Brunswick they cost $140 a tonne. The food processing companies which make the frozen French fries, the chicken pot pie dinners, and all the rest are simply saying that they will survive because capital can move. That is the story of the trade deal. This is a deal for big capital which can move and need not worry about boundaries. Mr. McLean put his finger on it. The workers cannot move, nor can the farmers. They have to stay on the land in their communities.
We admit that this deal favours corporate capital but it does not favour farmers or workers because they do not have that flexibility. They cannot push a button and move money around in seconds. This deal clearly discriminates and does not take into account that Canada is on the northern part of the continent, has a harsh winter climate, and must move things long distances, which involves transportation costs which must be paid for.

Over the years we have learned that if we want to be even close to self-sufficient in food, we must provide protection for the farmers and industries which provide that self-sufficiency in food. With one swoop under this agreement the Government, which totally disregards the reality of geography and climate, is going to eliminate those jobs and that procedure. It has nothing to do with the question of whether we are competitive or not or whether Canadians are innovative or not. It simply comes down to reality, a hard sort of reality, but that is what has made us different. We have fought the elements and conquered them. We have found ways of dealing with them and we have used the public sector to do it. We have used the public economy to provide for the means and instruments and policies to ensure we can survive and prosper on the northern part of the continent, and we have always done it in our own judicious way. The fact is that we are changing the right to make those decisions.

Mr. Speaker, if the Hon. Parliamentary Secretary believed what he was talking about, and if he believed that the SAG1TS that were appointed by the Government were meaningful and were going to do anything, the amendment before the House would have been contained
Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement
in the free trade deal. Mr. Archie McLean, who is a member of the agriculture and food processing industry was a member of SAGITS, and the SAGITS recommended that this be in the deal. However, the Government did not put it in the deal because the Americans did not want it in the deal. They want to take over the whole Canadian food processing industry.
If anyone looks at Mr. McLean's letter, he or she will see that 22 of the 26 largest food processing companies in Canada are American owned, for example, Proctor and Gamble, Nabisco, and so on. They do not want to process food in this country. They want to process it in the United States and ship into the Canadian market.
The Parliamentary Secretary talks about who is in favour of the deal. He should go down and talk to the UPA in Quebec. It is not in favour of the deal. He should talk to the Ontario Federation of Agriculture. It is not in favour of the deal. He should talk to the advisory board to the Canadian Wheat Board. On July 17 it passed a resolution in which it opposed the free trade agreement because it would undermine the ability of the Canadian Wheat Board to be an effective marketing agency on behalf of all Canadian grain growers.
There is a large number of Canadian agricultural groups extremely opposed to the agreement, but nobody is more concerned than the supply management sectors of the Canadian agriculture, the dairy producers and the poultry producers that operate in this country by an administered price. We have in place import and production controls, and we have the most healthy agricultural sector anywhere in western Europe or in North America because of our supply management system. Knowledgeable people who have looked at this deal believe that in the long run it will destroy our marketing board and supply management system.
There are two factors involved. First, there is a provision in the GATT agreement, Article 711, which provides the umbrella that allows us to have import controls. The Americans are going to GATT, as are the Cairns Group and others, stating that they want to get rid of that provision of the GATT. We say in this agreement that we are going to GATT, agreeing to get rid of all agricultural subsidies. Canadian farmers do not think of supply management as being a subsidy, but American farmers and the American Government believe that something like 50 per cent of the income of Canadian dairy farmers is considered a subsidy because it results from the supply management system. That is one aspect. When GATT sees us giving in on many of these things with the import controls and so on, that will be the next thing to fall in the GATT negotiations.
More important is the whole food processing industry. It believes if the tariff is removed on highly processed foods, such as Mr. McLean is stating, then it is much cheaper to process the food in the United States and bring it into Canada, because it is much cheaper to buy it in the United States. For instance, when he made a presentation to our caucus task force in February, 1988, in Fredericton, he stated that their plant

which produces pizza at Grand Falls in New Brunswick employed some 250 people. Because of the cost of the cheese used in that pizza production-and they are the largest producer in Canada of frozen pizza-they will simply have to move to the United States. There we lose 250 jobs.
That is typical of the whole system, unless a mechanism is put in place, as was recommended by the SAGITS and as is recommended in this amendment before us tonight, so that all highly processed food that has more than 10 per cent by weight of supply management products such as milk, cheese, butter, eggs, poultry, or turkey, is put on the import control list.
The Parliamentary Secretary talks about putting things on the import control list, such as the Government did for yoghurt and ice-cream. He did not say that they have ever negotiated any limit. They have put them on the import control list but there has been no limit applied. The United States has already appealed that to GATT. If we look at the drafting instructions which came out of the United States Congress, they have a hit list that says: "First of all, we think that you have made fairly good progress in this free trade deal, in knocking down the whole supply management system for poultry and eggs and turkeys and so on, but we want all those tariffs removed in the long haul".
There is no question about what the United States position is going to be at the MTN in Geneva. There is no question of how successful they were and how the Europeans were at the GATT on the wine industry.
This Government is going to GATT, supporting the United States, and saying: "We are going to GATT to get rid of all the subsidies". The United States has a mechanism called the PSM, the producer subsidy equivalent, which applies to our supply management. They are going there and saying: "We are getting rid of all subsidies in this negotiation of the GATT round". This very simple amendment did not come simply from the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry (Mr. Axworthy). It came from the Government's own advisory group. It is a small chink in the armour to try to maintain that supply management system. I do not believe that anybody can honestly look at what the Government is doing, first of all, by removing all tariffs on highly processed food, going to the GATT, saying that it is supporting the American position on Article XI, and really believing that it wants to maintain the supply management system. We are pretty sure that it does not. If we listen to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Andre), he says: "Yes, we want to get rid of it". If we listen to what the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) says at the OECD meetings, he says: "Yes, we want to get rid of supply management".
There is no question that if this Government were ever to implement this deal, if it were ever to be re-elected-and hopefully, for the benefit of Canadians farmers, neither one of
those things will ever occur-that the supply management system would be destroyed in Canada, because that is its policy. It is not honest enough to say it publicly, but that is clearly the direction it is taking.
It is very interesting to note that so many of the agricultural groups, in spite of all their tricks and so on, are on to them. I was very, very interested in the decision by the Canadian Wheat Board Advisory Committee to oppose it. I was interested in the Saskatchewan Pool voting 120 to 24 to reject supporting this free trade deal. People in the horticulture industry in British Columbia and Ontario are extremely concerned that their industry will be destroyed.
This is a good amendment. The Government should be accepting it.
